claims.text: Adding approximately 1 wt.% Y2O3 nanoparticles to a refractory high-entropy alloy can produce a uniform oxide dispersion.
The introduced oxide particulates will be distributed both at grain boundaries and within grains.
The dispersed oxide particulates act as sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
Y2O3 dispersoids attract and trap radiation-induced point defects.
Trapping point defects at Y2O3 dispersoids facilitates defect recombination.
Enhanced defect recombination mitigates irradiation-induced defect accumulation.
Reduced defect accumulation lowers irradiation-induced swelling.
Reduced defect accumulation lowers irradiation-induced hardening.
The Y2O3-modified alloy will have a lower post-irradiation defect density than the unmodified alloy.
The Y2O3-modified alloy will exhibit less irradiation-induced swelling than the unmodified alloy.
The Y2O3-modified alloy will exhibit less irradiation-induced hardening than the unmodified alloy.
The Y2O3-modified alloy will retain mechanical integrity under simulated fusion-reactor irradiation conditions.
The unmodified refractory high-entropy alloy typically experiences higher defect accumulation and associated mechanical degradation under irradiation.
The beneficial effect is expected to hold at reactor-relevant irradiation doses and temperatures around 1000 °C.
Extreme irradiation or prolonged high-temperature exposure may destabilize the dispersoids and diminish their benefits.
Existing evidence supports enhanced defect recombination through the use of oxide dispersoids.
